A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that the use of the multilevel human cervical cadaveric model is a valid and reproducible biomechanical testing method for assessing the kinematic and load-sharing characteristics of spinal arthroplasties in a multileveled cervical spine.

the use of a multilevel model with the addition of an anterior plating system provides an accurate biomechanical model that allows for a more realistic evaluation of cervical motion preserving devices.

the use of a multilevel cadaveric model is an effective method to evaluate cervical arthroplasty devices and that a multilevel model provides a better representation of the in vivo environment than single-level models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current testing protocol is not appropriate to assess the performance of cervical motion preserving devices.
the biomechanical testing of spinal implants should be performed in a multileveled human cadaveric model to provide a realistic representation of spinal motion in the clinical setting.
we have shown a new way to use a novel, noninvasive, imaging-based method to assess changes in the spine's biomechanical properties in response to spinal fusion.
